newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: LME zinc seen setting fresh highs - Asian trade.
newsitem.headline: LME zinc seen setting fresh highs - Asian trade.

text.p: Three-month zinc prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are expected to forge ahead later on Thursday on continuing pressure from funds and Wednesday's strong technical close near a seven-year high, traders said.
"We expect zinc prices will rise further on a squeeze by the funds," said a trader with a local brokerage firm.
Three-month zinc was barely changed at $1,470/$1,475 a tonne at 0400 GMT in Asian trade from Wednesday's late LME close.

LME broker Macquarie said in its daily report that "(the zinc market) has gapped higher on the charts and after Wednesday's strong technical performance, a test of resistance at $1,480 now looks likely."
But a Korean trader said zinc could see a correction in the near-term to the market's overbought situation.

The 14-day relative strength index (RSI) for three-month zinc rose to 76.24 percent on Wednesday from 71.60 percent the previous day. The market generally considers an RSI of 70 or more as overbought and 30 or less as oversold.
Macquarie said there was widespread talk in the zinc market of a squeeze being engineered by one major trade house possibly in association with some producers.

The "victims" of the are said to be Chinese producers who are variously describd as being short between 200,000-400,000 tonnes of the metal, the Macquarie report said. Other reports have said the Chinese have sold forward about 60,000 tonnes of zinc.
The Korean trader said the zinc market's supply/demand deficit had probably prompted a significant increase in Chinese exports of the metal in the first half of 1997.

Earlier this year Macquarie estimated the zinc market's deficit would be about 270,000 tonnes in 1997 and 130,000 tonnes in 1998. But the trader said tight zinc concentrate supplies would reduce Chinese exports in the second half.
Traders said a report that shipments of copper concentrates had resumed from the Ok Tedi copper mine in Papua New Guinea, following heavy rains, would put some pressure on the market.
A spokesman for Australia's Broken Hill Pty Ltd said on Thursday heavy rains have enabled the Ok Tedi mine to restart shipments of copper concentrates on the Fly River this week.

One of two grinding mills, shut down last month as drought conditions worsened at the remote mine site in the Western Province of PNG, has been restarted, although a second mill remains idle, the spokesman said.
Traders said benchmark three-month LME copper is expected to trade in a range of $2,350 to $2,450 a tonne near-term.
Three-month copper was flat at $2,417/$2,422 at 0400 GMT in thin Asian trade.
LME broker Brandeis said in its daily report the copper market needed to end above $2,440 a tonne to turn the charts more favourable.
Three-month aluminium bid prices rose slightly to $1,618 at 0530 GMT in Asian trade on Thursday from Wednesday's late LME close of $1,617.

Brandeis said after closing the gap on the chart between $1,608 and $1,612, the market had finished constructively. However, there were signs of indecision and aluminium really needed to breach $1,620 and then $1,635 for further upward momentum.
Support was seen at the 10-day moving average at $1,602, Brandeis said.
-- Jae Hur, Seoul Newsroom (822) 727 5651
